Optical Fiber: Multimode and Singlemode, Buffers, Jackets, and the Color Code

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 4 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

A reel arrives with an orange jacket and the drawing calls for aqua. Before the foreman swears, you check the print: fiber jacket color is a convention, and the real type is printed on the cable. To handle fiber you need to know its parts and its names.

Core, cladding, coating

Light travels in the core. The cladding around it bends the light back in, and is 125 micron on both multimode and singlemode. The coating protects the glass. A multimode core is 62.5 or 50 micron; a singlemode core is about 9 micron.

Type   Core         Jacket color
OM1    62.5 micron  orange
OM2    50 micron    orange
OM3    50 micron    aqua
OM4    50 micron    aqua (some violet)
OM5    50 micron    lime green
OS1/2  about 9      yellow

Buffers and cable styles

  • Tight buffer: a 900 micron coating on each fiber. Used inside buildings and easy to terminate.
  • Loose tube: 250 micron coated fibers floating in a gel or dry tube. Used outdoors and transitioned at the building entry.
  • Cables are made for indoor, outdoor, or indoor-outdoor use. Indoor-outdoor cable is built to survive both environments, so it needs no transition at the building entry.
  • Armored cable has a metal layer that resists crushing and rodents. Interlocking armor must be bonded to the telecom bonding system.

The 12-color code

Blue, orange, green, brown, slate, white, red, black, yellow, violet, rose, aqua. Fibers 13 to 24 repeat the colors with a black tracer; the black fiber takes a yellow tracer. Loose-tube cables color the buffer tubes with the same order, so you name a fiber by tube color and fiber color.

Light and handling

Multimode uses LED or VCSEL sources at 850 and 1300 nm. Singlemode uses a laser at 1310 and 1550 nm. Never look into a fiber end.

Tip: write the strand number on your pull sheet as you terminate. Colors fade in memory faster than on the buffer.
Exam tip: when jacket color and print disagree, believe the print. And remember: tight buffer indoors, loose tube outdoors.
Remember
Core, cladding, and coating make a fiber; OM1 to OM5 are multimode, OS1 and OS2 are singlemode, and the 12-color code names every strand.
Deeper explanation

Optical Fiber: Multimode and Singlemode, Buffers, Jackets, and the Color Code, explained slowly

Reading a fiber cable

A fiber cable has several layers, and every layer has a job. From the center out: the glass core and cladding (125 micron cladding in both families), a coating, a buffer, strength members, and a jacket. Knowing the order lets you strip it without cutting what you should not.

Layer              Job
Core               carries the light
Cladding           keeps the light in the core
Coating            protects the glass; 250 micron
Buffer             tight 900 micron, or loose tube
Strength member    aramid yarn that takes the pull
Jacket             outer protection and the printed identity

Matching type to system

Fiber         Source                Wavelengths     Typical use
OM1, OM2      LED                   850, 1300 nm    short older links
OM3, OM4      VCSEL                 850 nm          laser optimized links
OM5           VCSEL                 850 nm and wider  wideband links
OS1, OS2      laser                 1310, 1550 nm   long distance

The 12-color code, worked

Strands in order: Blue, Orange, Green, Brown, Slate, White, Red, Black, Yellow, Violet, Rose, Aqua. A 24-fiber cable has two groups: strands 1 to 12 in solid colors, and strands 13 to 24 in the same colors with a black tracer, except the black strand, which takes a yellow tracer.

Worked example: strand 15 is the third color of the second group, so it is green with a black tracer. Strand 20 is the eighth color, so it is black with a yellow tracer. A loose-tube cable with 6 tubes of 12 fibers colors the tubes with the same order, so fiber 5 of tube 3 is slate in a green tube.

Armor and bonding

Armored cable has a metal layer. Interlocking armor is bonded to the telecom bonding system at each end, because it is a conductive path that can carry fault current. Plain jackets need no bonding.

Jacket colors

Colors are voluntary and vary by maker, so a color on its own never tells you the type. Always read the print.

Remember: tight buffer inside, loose tube outside, and bond the armor.
